common_name: Royal Crown Magnolia (Dark Red-Violet Gresham Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in a site sheltered from late frost, since the goblet-shaped blooms open on bare wood before leaf-out.

directions: Royal Crown is one of the early D. Todd Gresham hybrids, a cross of Magnolia liliiflora and M. x veitchii first described in the Morris Arboretum Bulletin in 1962. Its twelve dark red-violet tepals form a tall, narrow bud that opens with the outer tepals folding sharply back, giving each bloom the stepped, pointed look of a crown. Plant in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and allow room for a broad-crowned small tree, since Gresham hybrids of this parentage tend to grow larger and more vigorously than the straight soulangeana cultivars most gardeners already know. Water deeply through the first two seasons and avoid heavy pruning, which magnolias tolerate poorly.

common_name: Royal Flush Magnolia (Dark-Based White Gresham Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, sheltered from hard late-winter frost that can scorch the earliest flower buds.

directions: Also raised by D. Todd Gresham and published alongside 'Royal Crown' in 1962, Royal Flush comes from the cross of Magnolia x soulangeana 'Lennei Alba' with M. x veitchii 'Peter Veitch'. The flowers are predominantly white but carry a dark red-violet stain at the base of each inner tepal, giving the open bloom a blushed, two-toned center rather than the solid color of many soulangeana selections. Grow it as a specimen tree in deep, fertile soil with consistent moisture during establishment, and site it away from low frost pockets where the early-opening flowers could be damaged. Because it is a vigorous Gresham-line hybrid, give it as much lateral room as a mature saucer magnolia.

common_name: Sayonara Magnolia (Late-Blooming White Gresham Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; because Sayonara flowers later than most saucer-type hybrids, it largely escapes the frost damage that affects earlier bloomers.

directions: Sayonara is a D. Todd Gresham hybrid of Magnolia x soulangeana 'Lennei Alba' and M. x veitchii 'Peter Veitch', documented in the Journal of the Royal Horticultural Society in the 1960s and still referenced in the current Magnolia Society cultivar register. It grows with a spreading, arching branch structure and produces globe-shaped white flowers with a soft rose-pink stain at the base, opening notably later in the season than most of its soulangeana relatives. The later bloom time is its main garden virtue, since it largely dodges the late frosts that can ruin an early magnolia display. Site it in full sun with well-drained, fertile soil and give it room to develop its naturally wide-spreading form.

common_name: Peppermint Stick Magnolia (Violet-Striped White Gresham Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltered from strong wind that can mar the thin-textured tepals.

directions: Bred by D. Todd Gresham from Magnolia liliiflora crossed with M. x veitchii, Peppermint Stick was first described in the Morris Arboretum Bulletin in 1962 and takes its name from the candy-striped pattern on its blooms. The flowers open mostly white with a violet-tinted base and violet striping running up the midrib of each tepal, while the outer tepals reflex back and the inner ones remain upright, creating a layered, two-tiered flower shape. Plant in fertile, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture, and treat it like other large-flowered magnolia hybrids by avoiding heavy pruning once established. It makes a striking specimen where the striped interior of the flower can be viewed from below or at eye level.

common_name: Frank Gladney Magnolia (Vigorous Deep Pink Gresham Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this vigorous Gresham hybrid benefits from a planting site with room for substantial size.

directions: Frank Gladney is another Magnolia liliiflora x M. x veitchii cross from hybridizer D. Todd Gresham, published in Magnolia, the journal of the Magnolia Society, in 1984. It is noted among the Gresham hybrids for its exceptional vigor and strongly upright growth habit, reaching tree size faster than many of its siblings. The large flowers, up to a foot across, are deep pink on the outside with a creamy white interior, carried on twelve broad, substantial tepals. Give it a permanent, open site in fertile, well-drained soil, since it quickly outgrows a cramped foundation planting and performs best as a freestanding specimen tree.

common_name: Jon Jon Magnolia (Dark Plum Young-Flowering Gresham Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Jon Jon flowers at a young age, often within a few years of planting.

directions: Jon Jon is a Gresham-line hybrid of Magnolia x soulangeana 'Lennei Alba' and M. x veitchii 'Peter Veitch' that holds an upright habit and some of the darkest coloring in the group, with flowers described as a deep, dark plum. Unlike many large-flowered magnolia hybrids that take a decade or more to bloom, Jon Jon begins flowering while still a young tree, which makes it a good choice for gardeners who want earlier payoff from a specimen planting. Set it in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun and mulch to keep the root zone cool and evenly moist. Prune only to correct crossing or damaged branches, since magnolias heal cuts slowly.

common_name: Apollo Magnolia (Two-Toned New Zealand Jury Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, sheltered from late frost that can damage the earliest flowers.

directions: Apollo was bred in New Zealand by Felix Jury as a sister seedling to the well-known 'Iolanthe', pairing an unnamed liliiflora-type seedling with Magnolia campbellii 'Lanarth'. It is a floriferous hybrid whose color shifts through the bloom season: the earliest flowers open deep violet-purple with paler interiors, while later flowers in the same display fade toward a deep rose-pink, giving an established tree a two-toned look over several weeks. The blooms carry a distinct fruity fragrance and can reach up to 10 inches across on a mature specimen. Plant in a sheltered, sunny site with fertile, well-drained soil, since the campbellii parentage makes the earliest buds vulnerable to hard late frosts.

common_name: Athene Magnolia (Ivory Cup-and-Saucer Jury Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Athene develops into a substantial tree, so allow room for its mature spread.

directions: Felix Jury raised Athene in New Zealand from a cross of Magnolia x soulangeana 'Lennei Alba' with his own earlier hybrid 'Mark Jury', producing a tree that reaches 20 to 25 feet in height at maturity. Its large cup-and-saucer flowers are ivory white with a violet-pink stain at the base of the tepals, opening to 8 to 10 inches across. It flowers reliably once established and makes a good anchor specimen where a classic saucer-magnolia look is wanted with a cooler, more restrained color than the common pink soulangeana cultivars. Grow it in moist, well-drained soil with consistent watering during the first several seasons.

common_name: Gold Star Magnolia (Creamy Yellow Star-Flowered Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; its compact upright habit suits smaller gardens better than many yellow-flowered magnolia hybrids.

directions: Hybridized by Phil Savage from Magnolia acuminata var. subcordata 'Miss Honeybee' and M. stellata 'Rubra', Gold Star combines a cucumbertree's yellow pigment with a star magnolia's narrow, many-tepaled flower form. New leaves emerge bronze-red before maturing to green, and the starlike flowers open creamy yellow with fourteen strap-shaped tepals to about 4 inches across, closer in form to a star magnolia than to the broader cups of most yellow hybrids. It grows as a small, upright tree, which makes it a more manageable choice for average-sized gardens than many of the larger yellow-flowered magnolia hybrids. Plant in moist, slightly acidic, well-drained soil and water regularly through establishment.

common_name: Golden Sun Magnolia (Strong Yellow Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade.

directions: Golden Sun was bred by noted Ohio hybridizer David G. Leach from a cross of Magnolia acuminata and M. denudata and introduced from his Madison, Ohio breeding grounds. Its dense, floriferous canopy produces strongly colored yellow flowers that open flat rather than cupped, reaching up to 7 inches across with prominent green calyces showing at the base of the six tepals. It grows vigorously and flowers at a comparatively young age for a yellow hybrid magnolia, making it a useful choice where an established-looking specimen is wanted sooner. Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil and avoid hot, exposed western sites, which can fade the yellow color.

common_name: Goldfinch Magnolia (Early Pale Yellow Hybrid Magnolia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; Goldfinch flowers very early, so choose a site away from frost pockets.

directions: Goldfinch is a Phil Savage hybrid of Magnolia acuminata var. subcordata 'Miss Honeybee' and M. denudata 'Sawada's Cream', bred in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan and published by the Magnolia Society in 1989. It grows into a tall, graceful, single-trunked tree rather than the shrubbier form of many yellow hybrids, and its light yellow flowers open very early in the season, sometimes alongside the first emerging leaves rather than strictly before them. Because the flowers appear so early, give it a planting site protected from late cold snaps and sheltered from harsh wind. Grow in moist, fertile, well-drained soil and allow the single leader to develop without heavy pruning.

common_name: Barbara Cook Magnolia (Exceptional Pink Dawson's Magnolia Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in a sheltered, sunny site away from frost pockets, since the early flowers open well before the leaves.

directions: Barbara Cook arose as a chance seedling in the Fort Bragg, California garden of Dr. Bowman and was later introduced into commerce by Briggs Nursery of Olympia, Washington. It was selected and named for the exceptional depth and clarity of its pink flower color, which stands out even among the generally fine pink tones typical of the species, and it was named in honor of noted Vancouver plantsman Alleyne Cook's wife. Like the wild species, it forms a large, long-lived tree and flowers on bare branches in late winter to early spring before the foliage emerges, so plant it in a sheltered site away from cold air drainage. Give it deep, fertile, well-drained soil and the room to grow into a substantial specimen over many decades.

common_name: Blood Moon Magnolia (Dark-Flowered Sargent's Magnolia Selection)

planting.note: Plant grafted or container-grown trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in a sheltered site away from frost pockets, since the early flowers open well before any leaf cover.

directions: Blood Moon is a selection of the Chinese species Magnolia sargentiana long cultivated at the Strybing Arboretum in San Francisco, traced back to material originating from Viscount Cranborne's collection. It is distinguished from typical sargentiana seedlings, which usually bloom rose-pink, by flowers that open in a notably darker, deeper wine tone, giving the tree a moodier and more dramatic late-winter display. Like the species, it forms a large, pendulous-flowered tree that needs decades to reach full size, so plant it in a spacious, sheltered site protected from late frost and strong wind. Grow in moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil and expect a slow but eventually massive specimen tree.

common_name: Dark Diva Magnolia (Hardy Dark-Flowered Sprenger's Magnolia Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltered from strong wind and late frost pockets.

directions: Dark Diva was selected by Phil Savage from seed collected at San Francisco's Strybing Arboretum and chosen for flowers darker in color and a constitution hardier than the typical 'Diva' clone of Magnolia sprengeri var. diva that most gardens grow. The large, fragrant blooms open deep pink to red-purple on bare branches in early to mid spring, ahead of the foliage, and the tree eventually becomes a broad, substantial specimen like other sprengeri selections. Because the improved cold tolerance is its main advantage over the standard 'Diva', it suits gardeners at the cooler edge of the species' range who still want its oversized, richly colored flowers. Site it away from cold air drainage and grow in fertile, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with consistent moisture.
